cf.title: md: measure just FileSync() for pgstat_io without FileClose()

input.subject: md: measure just FileSync() for pgstat_io without FileClose()

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2, so nothing ranked stops the patch. The change is confined to md.c and affects only the IOOP_FSYNC timing in pg_stat_io. Confidence is low because the thread has two messages, no measurement of close() time, and the code was not read.

brief.title: Exclude close() time from fsync timing in pg_stat_io
brief.problem: In mdsyncfiletag(), the time counted for IOOP_FSYNC can include the FileClose() call that follows FileSync(). The author asks whether close() time should be left out, so that fsync timing in pg_stat_io reflects only the fsync. The thread does not say who is affected or whether anyone has seen skewed numbers.
brief.proposed_design: The patch changes only md.c so that the IOOP_FSYNC duration covers FileSync() alone and no longer includes a possible close() system call. The commit message gives no further design detail.
user_visible_surface: Fsync timing for IOOP_FSYNC in pg_stat_io (with track_io_timing on) no longer includes close() time.
author_claims: The current IOOP_FSYNC duration may include the duration of an extra close() system call.
brief.thread_state: One reviewer, Zizhuan Liu, agrees that the timing should ideally cover only FileSync(). He doubts the change is needed, because his code reading finds no expensive cleanup in FileClose() for these handles, and he did no benchmark. The author has not replied.
unclear: The commit message does not say how the patch takes the end time of FileSync() before FileClose() with the current pgstat_count_io_op_time() interface.
The thread has no measurement showing that close() time is large enough to skew IOOP_FSYNC numbers.
The thread does not say whether pgaio_closing_fd() can block in FileClose() for these handles.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch changes how mdsyncfiletag() in md.c times IOOP_FSYNC for pg_stat_io.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: How does the patch take the end time of FileSync() before FileClose() with the current pgstat_count_io_op_time() interface?
Is there a measurement where close() time in mdsyncfiletag() changes the IOOP_FSYNC time in pg_stat_io by a visible amount?
Can pgaio_closing_fd() block in FileClose() for the file handles that mdsyncfiletag() opens and closes?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the pg_stat_io timing code and the md.c sync path would have to own it; no committer has spoken in the thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the meaning of the IOOP_FSYNC time in pg_stat_io, and for any new timing helper if the patch adds one.
committability.author_follow_up: The author moved the entry to the next CommitFest on 2026-10-01 but has not replied to message #2.

priority.reason: The patch is about 1 KiB in one file and affects only users who read fsync timing in pg_stat_io with track_io_timing on. It waits on an author reply to message #2 and on a committer who knows the area.

provisional_note: Without the code, it could not be checked whether the patch adds a new pgstat_count_io_op_time() variant or moves the FileClose() call. Whether close() time is ever large in this path also could not be judged.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fsync queue forgets requests on failure
precedents_retrieved.summary: Fix the checkpointer so that when an fsync of a relation segment fails during a checkpoint, the pending fsync request is kept for the next checkpoint instead of being dropped. The patch stops the pending-ops bitmapset from being lost when it is unlinked from the hashtable entry, merges unprocessed requests back on failure, and removes segments that succeeded as it goes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it as redundant with work in another thread (by Craig and Andres) that turns fsync I/O errors into PANICs and overhauls the request queue, because retrying fsync after a failure is useless on Linux. He noted that the other patch still left the retry path for errnos other than EIO and ENOSPC, but rejected this entry on the grounds that the issue would be resolved in that other thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Rejected, since this will have to be dealt with one way or another in
that other thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Unlogged relation copy is not fsync'd
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes the condition in RelationCopyStorage() so that the main and other non-init forks of an unlogged relation are fsync'd after copying, for example during alter table ... set tablespace. Without the fix, a checkpoint during the copy followed by a clean shutdown and power loss can lose part of the copied file.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author found that the posted patch was still incomplete and proposed a broader backpatchable fix that calls smgrimmedsync() for all but temporary relations, with similar changes in nbtsort.c, gistbuild.c and rewriteheap.c. Noah Misch questioned part of that analysis, and no revised patch followed. After about three months with no new version, Robert Haas marked the entry Returned with feedback as waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So it seems this has been waiting for
Heikki or someone else to have time to work it for the last 3 months.

precedents_retrieved.title: speed up pg_rewind by using copy_file_range() and skipping some fsync
precedents_retrieved.summary: Two pg_rewind patches: one syncs only the files pg_rewind changed instead of the whole target data directory, and one uses copy_file_range() in place of read()+write() for local rewinds. The second adds a configure check and HAVE_COPY_FILE_RANGE and falls back to read()+write() on EXDEV or ENOTSUP.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier asked for pg_rewind benchmarks: many small files for the fsync patch, and large and small file sets on XFS with reflink for copy_file_range(). He also asked to drop the copy_file_range_support flag, because one EXDEV failure would turn copy_file_range() off for all other tablespaces and mount points, and to fix double-counted progress on fallback. The fsync patch skips files such as configuration files included from postgresql.conf. The visible messages do not show a reply after his last review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Anyway, I think that it would be good to do more benchmarking for this
patch first, and the patch you are proposing is enough for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Show WAL stats on pg_stat_io
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds WAL I/O (writes, fsyncs, reads during recovery, and WAL segment initialization in a new IOCONTEXT_INIT) to the pg_stat_io view as IOOBJECT_WAL. Timings use track_wal_io_timing, and pg_stat_wal timings would come from pg_stat_io.
precedents_retrieved.objection: pg_stat_io ties op_bytes to a fixed block size per object and context, but some WAL reads, such as those by the WAL receiver, have a variable size. Reviewers did not agree whether to set op_bytes to 1, to NULL, or to add per-operation byte columns. Michael Paquier proposed to set the patch aside until WAL reads and writes, async I/O and cached reads are settled, so that the meaning of pg_stat_io does not change between releases. The author agreed, and the patch was marked Returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
IMHO, perhaps we'd better put this patch aside until we are absolutely
*sure* of what we want to achieve when it comes to WAL, and I am
afraid that this cannot happen until we're happy with the way we
handle WAL reads *and* writes, including WAL receiver or anything that
has the idea of pulling its own page callback with
XLogReaderAllocate() in the backend.

precedents_retrieved.title: s/shm_mq_iovec/struct iovec/
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the shm_mq module's own shm_mq_iovec struct with the standard POSIX struct iovec. The motivation was to remove a duplicate definition now that struct iovec can be used everywhere.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas argued that the two structs belong to separate APIs and should stay separate. Reusing struct iovec could tie shm_mq to POSIX limits such as IOV_MAX, and it would stop shm_mq from adding its own fields later. The author accepted this and marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
They serve a similar purpose,
but they belong to completely separate APIs; I think "incidental
deduplication" is the right term for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Asynchronous and "direct" IO support for PostgreSQL
precedents_retrieved.authors: Andres Freund (andresfreund), David Rowley (davidrowley), Thomas Munro (macdice)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Andres Freund proposed an asynchronous IO (AIO) subsystem for Postgres, with several backends (worker processes, io_uring, posix AIO, Windows) and helpers for streaming reads and writes. The same work adds optional direct IO, so data moves between storage and shared buffers without the kernel page cache.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry died of inactivity. The patch set stopped applying in January 2022 and no rebased version followed. In May 2022 Aleksander Alekseev asked for a rebase and said a set of 39 patches was too large to review, and that it should be split. Michael Paquier marked it Returned with feedback after five months without activity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't know what's the exact status here, but as there has been no
activity for the past five months, I have just marked the entry as RwF
for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Get rid of pgstat_count_backend_io_op*() functions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the pgstat_count_backend_io_op*() functions, so I/O counters are incremented once, and copies the pending I/O stats into the per-backend pending stats when the I/O stats flush. To make this work, per-backend stats must flush after the other stats kinds, first by placing PGSTAT_KIND_BACKEND last in the enum and later (v3) by flushing it outside the loop in pgstat_report_stat().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected to the ordering dependency between stats kinds at flush time, which so far have been independent, and said the copy approach hurts readability. He also said there was no benchmark data to choose among inlining, static structures, copies or fewer diffs, so the picture was incomplete. Andres Freund rejected the alternative WalUsage-style diff approach as too costly. The thread ends with the author disagreeing, and the visible messages do not show a final decision.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Hmm.  I really have an issue with the ordering dependency this
introduces between stats kinds, assumed to happen inside the code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Enhance statistics reset functions to return reset timestamp
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Michael Paquier, Andres Freund, David Rowley
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make the core statistics reset functions, such as pg_stat_reset(), pg_stat_reset_shared() and pg_stat_reset_replication_slot(), return the reset time as timestamptz, as pg_stat_statements_reset() already does. Functions that take a backend PID or slot name would return NULL for invalid input.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patches after objections. Michael Paquier said most of these functions never fail, and the reset time is already in the stats views. Andres Freund saw no convincing use case and said granular resets were a mistake to build on. David Rowley agreed, said that resetting stats to track activity is wrong and can affect autovacuum, and suggested logging values and taking differences with LAG().
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
-1 - I think it was a mistake to introduce support for granular resets, we
shouldn't bury ourselves deeper.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add redo LSN to pgstats files"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add redo LSN to pgstats files"
Reverted commit(s): Add redo LSN to pgstats files
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit b860848232aa, that was added as a prerequisite for
the support of pgstats data flush across checkpoints, linking a pgstats
file to a specific checkpoint redo LSN.

As reported, this is proving to be currently problematic when going
through a pg_upgrade, that does direct manipulations of the control file
in the new cluster.  The LSN stored in the pgstats file is not able to
cope with any changes done in the control file by pg_upgrade yet,
causing the pgstats file to be discarded when starting the new cluster
after overriding its redo LSN (one is a `pg_resetwal -l` where the new
cluster's start LSN is bumped by a hardcoded value of 8 segments, see
copy_xact_xlog_xid).

The least painful path going forward is likely going to be a refactor of
the pgstats code so as it is possible to read and write some of its data
with some routines in src/common/, so as pg_upgrade or pg_resetwal are
able to update its data.  The main point is that we are going to need a
LSN in the stats file should we make it written at checkpoint time and
not only as part of a shutdown sequence.  It is too late to dive into
these details for v18, so let's revert the change, and let's try to
figure out all the details in the next release cycle.  The pgstats file
is currently only written as part of a shutdown sequence, and its
contents are still lost on crash, same as older releases.

Bump PGSTAT_FILE_FORMAT_ID.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Disallow infinite endpoints in generate_series() for timestamps."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Disallow infinite endpoints in generate_series() for timestamps."
Reverted commit(s): Disallow infinite endpoints in generate_series() for timestamps.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit eafdf9de06e9b60168f5e47cedcfceecdc6d4b5f
and its back-branch counterparts.  Corey Huinker pointed out that
we'd discussed this exact change back in 2016 and rejected it,
on the grounds that there's at least one usage pattern with LIMIT
where an infinite endpoint can usefully be used.  Perhaps that
argument needs to be re-litigated, but there's no time left before
our back-branch releases.  To keep our options open, restore the
status quo ante; if we do end up deciding to change things, waiting
one more quarter won't hurt anything.

Rather than just doing a straight revert, I added a new test case
demonstrating the usage with LIMIT.  That'll at least remind us of
the issue if we forget again.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the precedent list has no row that proposes the same or a similar change, and the thread does not mention an earlier discussion of the idea. Without a recorded earlier rejection, the prior-attempts angle has no objection to raise.

From the standards and compatibility angle there is nothing to object to. The patch adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object or psql change, and adds nothing to dump. The only visible effect is slightly smaller IOOP_FSYNC times in pg_stat_io with track_io_timing on, and that is a fix to what the column is documented to measure. Whether the change is needed at all is a desirability question for another angle.

The patch changes only how md.c times IOOP_FSYNC for pg_stat_io. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or replication state. Cumulative stats are not replicated, and the brief names no change to the stats file format. A changed pgstat_count_io_op_time() signature could affect extensions, but the material does not show one.

The patch only changes which call the IOOP_FSYNC duration in pg_stat_io covers, inside md.c. It adds no new privilege, view, column, setting or exposure, and does not change who can read pg_stat_io. So there is no security or privilege aspect to object to.

From the maintenance angle this is a one-file change in md.c with no new GUC, catalog entry, external dependency or cost on a common path. The prose does not say whether it needs a new pgstat_count_io_op_time() variant that takes an end time; that cannot be checked without the code, and it would be the only new internal API.

No existing feature, view, GUC or extension gives an IOOP_FSYNC duration in pg_stat_io that leaves out close() time. The wait event WAIT_EVENT_DATA_FILE_SYNC covers FileSync() only, but it gives sampled wait state, not the cumulative pg_stat_io timing that the patch changes. The patch fixes how an existing counter is measured and adds no second mechanism, so this angle has no objection.

The thread shows no demand beyond one question, and no measurement that close() time skews IOOP_FSYNC. But the change is a small accuracy fix confined to md.c and paid for only by fsync timing, so it has no cost that falls on everyone and no concrete failure scenario. A committer would more likely ask for a short measurement, or for the reasoning about whether pgaio_closing_fd() can block in this path, than reject the patch for lack of users.
